questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Differentiating a relation with respect to time
questions.learningObjective: justify differentiating a constraint with respect to time
questions.stem: Explain what makes it legitimate to differentiate a geometric constraint with respect to time when the constraint was written without any time variable, and state what must be true of the quantities for the step to be valid.

answer.exemplar: A geometric constraint such as x^2 + y^2 = 400 describes the position of a moving object at every instant of its motion, even though no variable t appears in the written formula. Because the object keeps moving, each coordinate is really a function of t, and the constraint is a rule that the functions x(t) and y(t) satisfy at every value of t. Differentiating an equation that holds identically for all t is legitimate precisely because it holds for all t: the time derivative of each side describes how the two sides change together, and the chain rule supplies the factors dx/dt and dy/dt wherever x and y appear. What must be true is that the constraint holds at every instant of the motion rather than at just one instant, and that the quantities in it are differentiable functions of time. If a relation held only at a single instant, its derivative would say nothing about the motion, which is why substituting the instant's values before differentiating destroys the information. The result, 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0, is a new statement about rates that follows from the geometry and that stays valid exactly as long as the motion does.

questions.explanation: A constraint without an explicit t still holds at every instant once the quantities are read as functions of time, so it can be differentiated with respect to t. The chain rule then supplies the rate factors that make the differentiated equation a statement about rates.
questions.hint: Ask what it means for a written constraint to hold at every instant of a motion.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Differentiating a relation with respect to time
questions.learningObjective: compute the rate of change of distance from the origin along a curve
questions.stem: A point moves along the parabola y = x^2 so that dx/dt = 3. Find the rate at which its distance from the origin changes, in units per second, when x = 1. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: At x = 1 the point is (1,1), so D = sqrt(1 + 1) = sqrt(2). Differentiating D^2 = x^2 + y^2 with respect to t gives 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 2D(dD/dt), and since dy/dt = 2x(dx/dt) = 6 we get 2(1)(3) + 2(1)(6) = 18 on the left, so dD/dt = 18/(2 sqrt(2)) = 6.364 units per second. A second route substitutes y = x^2 to get D^2 = x^2 + x^4, differentiates to (2x + 4x^3)(dx/dt) = 2D(dD/dt), and at x = 1 gives 6(3) = 2 sqrt(2)(dD/dt), the same value.
questions.hint: Work with D^2 = x^2 + y^2 so that the square root is avoided.

questions.topic: Differentiating a relation with respect to time
questions.learningObjective: compute the rate of change of surface area of a growing sphere
questions.stem: A sphere's radius grows at 0.5 m/s. Find the rate of change of its surface area in square metres per second when r = 4 m. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Differentiating S = 4 pi r^2 with respect to t gives dS/dt = 8 pi r (dr/dt) = 8 pi (4)(0.5) = 16 pi, which is 50.265 square metres per second. A second route differentiates S with respect to r to get dS/dr = 8 pi r = 32 pi at r = 4 and then multiplies by dr/dt = 0.5 to reach 16 pi.
questions.hint: Differentiate the surface area formula with respect to t, not with respect to r.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a dropped rate factor in an area computation
questions.stem: For a growing circle a student writes dA/dt = 2 pi r and reports the surface area 8 pi when r = 4. What is the error?

options.text: The chain rule factor dr/dt is missing, so the expression is a derivative, not a rate per unit time
The exponent of r was lowered incorrectly, and the result should have been pi r^2 (dr/dt)
options.misconception: mis-applies the power rule and lowers the exponent by two instead of one

options.text: The formula should have been dA/dt = 2 pi r^2, since the area of a circle contains r squared
options.misconception: differentiates the area formula rather than the relation between the rates

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because a problem that gives only r is asking for a derivative, not a rate
options.misconception: confuses a derivative with respect to r with a rate of change with respect to t

questions.explanation: The correct expression is dA/dt = 2 pi r (dr/dt), and a numerical value can only be reported once dr/dt is known. Writing 2 pi r alone produces a quantity with units of length, which cannot be an area rate, and the dimensional mismatch is the fastest way to spot the error.
questions.hint: Check whether the reported expression has units of area per unit time.

options.text: V = pi r h^2, raising the height to the second power as though it were the radius

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why the differentiated equation holds at each instant of the motion
questions.stem: Explain why a relation between two changing quantities can be differentiated with respect to time even though the relation was written without any t, and what the resulting equation tells you that the original did not.

answer.exemplar: A relation like x^2 + y^2 = 400 is a statement about two positions that are true simultaneously, and when the motion is happening those positions are not fixed numbers but values of functions of time. Reading x and y as x(t) and y(t) turns the written relation into an identity in t that is satisfied at every instant the motion follows, so it is legitimate to differentiate both sides with respect to t. What the differentiated equation adds is a statement about rates: it says how quickly the two quantities have to change together so that the original relation keeps holding. That information is now about change rather than position, and it is what lets a known rate determine an unknown one. The differentiated equation is true for exactly the same instants as the original because it follows from the original by a rule that preserves truth, and it holds whether or not a particular instant has been chosen. Choosing an instant then only replaces x and y by numbers, producing a single linear equation for the unknown rate.

questions.explanation: Because the quantities are functions of time the relation holds at every instant as an identity in t, so differentiating with respect to t is valid and yields a statement about rates rather than about positions.
questions.hint: Think of x and y as x(t) and y(t) rather than as numbers.

questions.learningObjective: differentiate a relation whose constant appears under an exponent
questions.stem: A quantity satisfies e^y = x with dx/dt = 12. Which expression gives dy/dt?

options.text: dy/dt = (dx/dt)/x = 12/x, because differentiating e^y gives e^y (dy/dt) and e^y equals x
dy/dt = 12 e^y, because the derivative of e^y is e^y and it multiplies the given rate
options.misconception: multiplies by the rate instead of dividing, which breaks the equality of the two sides

options.text: dy/dt = 12, because the exponential relation removes the need for a chain rule factor
options.misconception: drops the factor dy/dt that the chain rule contributes to the exponential term

options.text: dy/dt = x/12, because the rate must be inverted when it appears in a denominator
options.misconception: inverts the rate of x instead of inverting the derivative of the exponential

questions.explanation: Differentiating e^y = x with respect to t gives e^y (dy/dt) = dx/dt, and since e^y = x this becomes x (dy/dt) = 12, so dy/dt = 12/x. A second route takes y = ln(x), giving dy/dt = (1/x)(dx/dt) = 12/x, the same expression.
questions.hint: Differentiate the exponential with the chain rule and then replace e^y by x.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: compute a volume rate for a cylinder of changing radius and height
questions.stem: A cylinder's radius grows at 1 m/s and its height grows at 2 m/s. Find dV/dt in cubic metres per second when r = 3 m and h = 5 m. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Differentiating V = pi r^2 h with respect to t gives dV/dt = pi (2 r h (dr/dt) + r^2 (dh/dt)). Substituting r = 3, h = 5, dr/dt = 1 and dh/dt = 2 gives pi (2(3)(5)(1) + 9(2)) = pi (30 + 18) = 48 pi, which is 150.796 cubic metres per second. A second route treats r^2 and h separately, using d(r^2)/dt = 2r(dr/dt) = 6 and dh/dt = 2 to get dV/dt = pi (6 h + 2 r^2) = pi (30 + 18) = 48 pi.
questions.hint: Use the product rule on r^2 h and note that both r and h carry rate factors.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a dimensional error in a reported rate
questions.stem: A student's answer for the height rate in a tank problem reads 2.5 m^2/s. Why is this answer wrong without any further calculation?

options.text: A height rate has units of length per time, so a rate with units of area per time is dimensionally wrong
The answer is fine, because units can be simplified later once the numeric value is known
options.misconception: treats units as decoration rather than as part of the quantity being reported

options.text: The answer is wrong only if the volume rate was given in cubic metres, which is not stated
options.misconception: makes the dimensional check conditional on information that the units already settle

options.text: The answer is wrong only if a radius appears in the problem statement somewhere.
options.misconception: ties the units of the answer to the presence of one variable rather than to the quantity asked for

questions.explanation: A rate of change of a length must have units of length per unit time, so an answer measured in square metres per second cannot be a height rate. Checking the units first catches this error before any arithmetic is redone, and it usually points to a missing division by the base area.
questions.hint: Compare the units of the reported answer with the units of the quantity that was requested.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: compute a shadow length rate using similar triangles
questions.stem: A 1.8 m tall person walks away from a 6 m lamppost at 1.5 m/s. Find the rate at which the person's shadow lengthens, in metres per second. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: With s the shadow length and d the distance from the post, similar triangles give 1.8/s = 6/(d + s), so 1.8(d + s) = 6s and 1.8 d = 4.2 s, hence s = (3/7) d and ds/dt = (3/7)(1.5) = 0.642857, which is 0.6429 metres per second. A second route writes h/(H - h) = 1.8/4.2 = 3/7 as the constant of proportionality between the shadow and the distance, giving the same 0.6429.
questions.hint: Set up the similar-triangle relation between the shadow, the person and the lamppost.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Differentiating a relation with respect to time
questions.learningObjective: differentiate a relation with respect to time and identify the unknown rate
questions.stem: A point moves on y = x^3 with dx/dt known. Why does the differentiated equation determine dy/dt at every instant along the curve?

options.text: Because the differentiated equation is linear in dy/dt, so it can be solved once x and dx/dt are given
Because dy/dt must equal dx/dt at every point of the curve, whatever the motion does
options.misconception: asserts an equality of rates that only holds on a line of slope one

options.text: Because the original equation fixes y completely, and a fixed quantity has a fixed rate
options.misconception: treats a quantity determined by another as unchanging

options.text: Because the differentiated equation contains no reference to x, so the position never matters
options.misconception: claims the position drops out of an equation that plainly depends on x

questions.explanation: Differentiating y = x^3 gives 3x^2(dx/dt) as an explicit value for dy/dt in terms of x and dx/dt, so once the position and the rate of x are known the rate of y is determined. The differentiated equation is linear in dy/dt, which is why a single known rate suffices.
questions.hint: Ask how many unknown quantities remain in the differentiated equation.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: compute a rate of change of volume for an expanding sphere
questions.stem: A sphere's radius increases at 0.4 mm/s. Find the rate at which its volume increases, in cubic millimetres per second, when r = 6 mm. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Differentiating V = (4/3) pi r^3 gives dV/dt = 4 pi r^2 (dr/dt) = 4 pi (36)(0.4) = 57.6 pi, which is 180.956 cubic millimetres per second. A second route computes dV/dr = 4 pi r^2 = 144 pi at r = 6 and multiplies by dr/dt = 0.4 to reach 57.6 pi.
questions.hint: Differentiate the sphere volume with respect to t and keep the factor dr/dt.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an error that confuses the radius with the depth in a cone
questions.stem: A student solves a conical tank problem by writing V = (1/3) pi h^3 and then dh/dt using the full tank depth. Which statement describes the flaw correctly?

options.text: The formula assumes the water radius equals the depth, which holds only when similar triangles force r = h
The formula is exactly right, since every inverted cone has radius equal to its depth
options.misconception: asserts a universal proportion that only some cones satisfy

options.text: The error is that the depth should have been replaced by the tank's top radius instead
options.misconception: swaps one dimension for another without fixing the hidden assumption about r

options.text: The error is that a cone's volume should not involve any depth at all.
options.misconception: denies the presence of the depth in the correct cone volume formula

questions.explanation: Substituting into V = (1/3) pi r^2 h to remove r requires the actual relation between r and h from similar triangles, such as r = h/3. Writing (1/3) pi h^3 silently sets r = h, which changes the coefficient in the differentiated equation and gives a wrong depth rate.
questions.hint: Ask what relation between r and h is being assumed by the formula you just wrote.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Differentiating a relation with respect to time
questions.learningObjective: differentiate a relation containing a square root with respect to time
questions.stem: A quantity satisfies y = sqrt(2 x) with dx/dt = 6. Find dy/dt in units per second when x = 8. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Writing y = sqrt(2 x) gives dy/dt = (1/sqrt(2 x)) (dx/dt) = (1/sqrt(16))(6) = 6/4 = 1.5 units per second. A second route squares to get y^2 = 2 x, differentiates to 2y(dy/dt) = 2(dx/dt), so dy/dt = (dx/dt)/y = 6/4 = 1.5 since y = 4 when x = 8.
questions.hint: Square the relation to remove the square root, or differentiate the square root directly.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a units check locates a missing operation in a rate computation
questions.stem: Explain how a check on the units of an answer can reveal that a step such as dividing by the base area was omitted, and describe the units that would give the mistake away.

answer.exemplar: A related rates answer carries the units of the quantity being computed divided by units of time, so a rate for a height must come out in metres per second or metres per minute, never in square metres per anything. The tallest test is to work out what those units force on the arithmetic: if the depth rate is wanted, then the formula dV/dt = pi r^2 (dh/dt) shows that a volume rate must be divided by an area to yield a length rate, because cubic metres per minute divided by square metres leaves metres per minute. A computation that omits the division produces an answer whose units are still cubic metres per minute, and that outcome is visible before any numbers are written down. Multiplying instead of dividing gives units that are even more obviously wrong, since an area times a volume rate cannot collapse to a length per time. The check is powerful because units cannot be faked: if the intermediate factors are not arranged so that everything except the length and the time cancels, no amount of algebra will produce a valid depth rate.

questions.explanation: A related rates answer must carry the units of the requested quantity per unit of time, so the units of each intermediate factor determine exactly which operations are permitted. Omitting a division by the base area leaves volume units in an answer that should have length units.
questions.hint: Compare the units of the given volume rate with the units that the requested rate must have.
